rows: The three moduli are not independent

questions.question: Q1. State Hooke's law and define the force constant.
questions.answer: Within the elastic limit, extension is proportional to the applied force: F ∝ x, or F = kx. The force constant k = F/x has unit N/m.
questions.shortcut: k = F/x (stiffer → larger k); plot F vs x is a straight line.
questions.example: A spring stretching 2 cm under 4 N → k = 4/0.02 = 200 N/m.

questions.question: Q2. Define stress and strain.
questions.answer: Stress = internal restoring force per unit area, σ = F/A (Pa). Strain = fractional change in dimension, ε (dimensionless). Elastic modulus E = stress/strain.
questions.shortcut: stress = F/A ; strain = ΔL/L ; E = σ/ε.
questions.example: A 10 N load on 2 m² gives 5 Pa of stress.

questions.question: Q3. Explain elastic limit and plastic region on a stress-strain curve.
questions.answer: Below the elastic limit the material returns to its original shape on unloading. Beyond the elastic (limiting proportional) point into the plastic region, some deformation is permanent. The fracture point is where it breaks.
questions.example: Rubber returns; a bent metal rod keeps its kink.

questions.question: Q4. A wire of cross-section 2 mm² and 1.5 m long stretches 1 mm under a 30 N load. Find E (Young's modulus).
questions.answer: Strain = ΔL/L = 0.001/1.5; stress = 30/(2×10⁻⁶)=1.5×10⁷ Pa. E = stress/strain = (1.5×10⁷)/(6.67×10⁻⁴) ≈ 2.25×10¹⁰ Pa ≈ 2.3×10¹⁰ N/m². ▥ 8.1 Hooke's Law & 8.2 Stress-Strain  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Stress vs Strain ▣ 8.3 Moduli of Elasticity

questions.question: Q5. Define Young's modulus, bulk modulus and shear modulus.
questions.answer: Young's modulus E = tensile stress/linear strain (stretching). Bulk modulus B = pressure/volumetric strain (compression). Shear modulus G = shear stress/shear strain (sliding layers).
questions.shortcut: E: length; B: volume; G: shape.
questions.example: Steel has high E, B and G (very elastic).

questions.question: Q6. A gas is compressed at constant pressure P with volume change ΔV/V. Find bulk modulus B.
questions.answer: B = P/(−ΔV/V) = P V/|ΔV|; for an ideal gas under isothermal compression B equals the pressure P.
questions.example: Doubling the compression halves B for a given P.

questions.question: Q7. State the relation between E, B and G.
questions.answer: E = 9BG / [3(3B + G)]. This lets you find one modulus if the other two are known. ▥ 8.3 Moduli of Elasticity  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Three Elastic Moduli at a Glance ▣ 8.4 Poisson's Ratio & 8.5 Elastic Potential Energy
questions.example: For a material with B=G, E = 9G/12 = ¾... (use formula).

questions.question: Q8. Define Poisson's ratio and give its typical value.
questions.answer: Poisson's ratio σ = (−lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain), the ratio of transverse contraction to axial extension. It is dimensionless; for most metals σ ≈ 0.25–0.3.
questions.example: A stretched thin rod gets narrower; σ≈0.3.

questions.question: Q9. Derive the elastic potential energy in a stretched wire.
questions.answer: Work = area under F–x graph = ½F·Δx (linear F–x). So U = ½kx² = ½(F/Δx)(Δx)² = ½FΔx. Energy density = ½(stress)(strain) = ½Eε².
questions.example: A 100 N force stretching a spring by 0.1 m stores 5 J.

questions.question: Q10. Find the strain energy stored in a wire with stress 2×10⁸ Pa, strain 0.002 and volume 5×10⁻⁵ m³.
Q11. Explain why a rubber band feels warm when stretched and cools on release.
questions.answer: Stretching increases molecular order (and lowers entropy); releasing lets the molecules gain entropy and the temperature drop. Rubber's elasticity is largely entropy-driven, so mechanical work interconverts with heat.
questions.shortcut: Rubber elasticity ≈ entropic (temperature rises on stretch).
questions.example: Snap a band fast; it is warmer for a moment.

questions.question: Q12. A 20 N load stretches a spring by 4 cm. Find the force constant and stored energy.
questions.answer: k = F/x = 20/0.04 = 500 N/m. U = ½kx² = ½(500)(0.04)² = 0.4 J. ▥ 8.4 Poisson's Ratio & 8.5 Elastic Potential Energy  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Moduli Relation + Elastic Energy PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T1. Derive the stress-strain relationship and Young's modulus.
theoryItems.answer: Stress = F/A (Pa); strain = ΔL/L (dimensionless). Young's modulus E = stress/strain = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL), a material constant in the elastic range.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T2. Derive the elastic potential energy stored in a stretched wire.
theoryItems.answer: Work = area under the F–x graph = ½F·Δx (linear F–x). So U = ½kx² = ½(F/Δx)(Δx)²; energy density u = ½(stress)(strain) = ½Eε².
theoryItems.example: A 100 N force stretching a spring 0.1 m stores 5 J.

theoryItems.question: [State] T3. State Hooke's law and define the force constant.
theoryItems.answer: Within the elastic limit, extension is proportional to the applied force: F ∝ x, or F = kx. The force constant k = F/x (N/m) measures the stiffness of the spring.
theoryItems.example: A 10 N force stretching 0.05 m → k = 200 N/m.

theoryItems.question: [Compare] T4. Compare elastic and plastic deformation with examples.
theoryItems.answer: Elastic: temporary, the body returns to its original shape on unloading (within the elastic limit). Plastic: permanent; the body retains the deformation beyond the yield point. Steel can elastically behave up to a high stress; putty is essentially plastic.
theoryItems.example: A bent-back-to-shape wire = elastic; a crumpled can = plastic.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T5. Explain the three elastic moduli (Young, bulk, shear).
theoryItems.answer: Young's E: tensile/linear strain (stretching). Bulk B: pressure/volumetric strain (compression). Shear G: tangential/shear strain (shape change). Each = the relevant stress/strain in the elastic limit.
theoryItems.shortcut: E: length; B: volume; G: shape.
theoryItems.example: A wire stretches (E), a ball compresses (B), a card shears (G).

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain Poisson's ratio and its typical value.
theoryItems.answer: Poisson's ratio σ = (−lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain), the fractional transverse contraction per axial extension. It is dimensionless; most metals σ ≈ 0.25–0.3, rubber near 0.5.
theoryItems.example: Stretching a thin wire makes it slightly thinner.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain the stress-strain curve, identifying the key regions.
theoryItems.answer: From the origin: linear (Hooke) region up to the proportional limit; elastic region up to the elastic limit; the upper/lower yield points; plastic (permanent) region; ultimate stress; fracture. The area under the curve = toughness (energy to break).
theoryItems.example: A ductile material shows a long plastic region.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T8. Explain the uses of elastic moduli in engineering design.
theoryItems.answer: E ensures a beam/column does not stretch or sag beyond tolerance; B and G determine resistance to compression (hydraulic fluids) and shear (girders); these guide material choice and safe load limits in bridges and buildings.
theoryItems.shortcut: E, B, G set deformation limits for safe design.
theoryItems.example: A high-E steel is chosen for a long beam's rigidity.

theoryItems.question: [Why] T9. Why does a rubber band feel warm when stretched and cool on release?
theoryItems.answer: Rubber's elasticity is largely entropic: stretching orders the polymer chains (reduces entropy), so it heats; releasing lets the chains gain entropy and it cools. Hence mechanical work interconverts with heat.
theoryItems.example: Snap a stretched band quickly; it is warmer briefly.

▣ 8.1 Hooke's Law & 8.2 Stress-Strain
Q1. State Hooke's law and define the force constant.
Answer:  Within the elastic limit, extension is proportional to the applied force: F ∝ x, or F = kx. The force constant k = F/x has unit N/m.
⚡ Shortcut:  k = F/x (stiffer → larger k); plot F vs x is a straight line.
Example:  A spring stretching 2 cm under 4 N → k = 4/0.02 = 200 N/m.
Q2. Define stress and strain.
Answer:  Stress = internal restoring force per unit area, σ = F/A (Pa). Strain = fractional change in dimension, ε (dimensionless). Elastic modulus E = stress/strain.
⚡ Shortcut:  stress = F/A ; strain = ΔL/L ; E = σ/ε.
Example:  A 10 N load on 2 m² gives 5 Pa of stress.
Q3. Explain elastic limit and plastic region on a stress-strain curve.

Answer:  Below the elastic limit the material returns to its original shape on unloading. Beyond the elastic (limiting proportional) point into the plastic region, some deformation is permanent. The fracture point is where it breaks.
⚡ Shortcut:  Elastic → returns; Plastic → stays deformed.
Example:  Rubber returns; a bent metal rod keeps its kink.
Q4. A wire of cross-section 2 mm² and 1.5 m long stretches 1 mm under a 30 N load. Find E (Young's modulus).
Answer:  Strain = ΔL/L = 0.001/1.5; stress = 30/(2×10⁻⁶)=1.5×10⁷ Pa. E = stress/strain = (1.5×10⁷)/(6.67×10⁻⁴) ≈ 2.25×10¹⁰ Pa ≈ 2.3×10¹⁰ N/m².
⚡ Shortcut:  E = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL).
Example:  ≈ 2.3×10¹⁰ Pa, typical for a metal.

▣ 8.3 Moduli of Elasticity
Q5. Define Young's modulus, bulk modulus and shear modulus.
Answer:  Young's modulus E = tensile stress/linear strain (stretching). Bulk modulus B = pressure/volumetric strain (compression). Shear modulus G = shear stress/shear strain (sliding layers).
⚡ Shortcut:  E: length; B: volume; G: shape.
Example:  Steel has high E, B and G (very elastic).
Q6. A gas is compressed at constant pressure P with volume change ΔV/V. Find bulk modulus B.
Answer:  B = P/(−ΔV/V) = P V/|ΔV|; for an ideal gas under isothermal compression B equals the pressure P.
⚡ Shortcut:  B = P/(ΔV/V).
Example:  Doubling the compression halves B for a given P.
Q7. State the relation between E, B and G.
Answer:  E = 9BG / [3(3B + G)]. This lets you find one modulus if the other two are known.
⚡ Shortcut:  E = 9BG/[3(3B+G)].
Example:  For a material with B=G, E = 9G/12 = ¾... (use formula).
▥ 8.3 Moduli of Elasticity  —  Compare / Contrast Tables

▣ 8.4 Poisson's Ratio & 8.5 Elastic Potential Energy
Q8. Define Poisson's ratio and give its typical value.
Answer:  Poisson's ratio σ = (−lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain), the ratio of transverse contraction to axial extension. It is dimensionless; for most metals σ ≈ 0.25–0.3.
⚡ Shortcut:  σ = lateral strain / longitudinal strain.
Example:  A stretched thin rod gets narrower; σ≈0.3.
Q9. Derive the elastic potential energy in a stretched wire.
Answer:  Work = area under F–x graph = ½F·Δx (linear F–x). So U = ½kx² = ½(F/Δx)(Δx)² = ½FΔx. Energy density = ½(stress)(strain) = ½Eε².
⚡ Shortcut:  U = ½Fx = ½kx² ; u = ½σ·ε.
Example:  A 100 N force stretching a spring by 0.1 m stores 5 J.
Q10. Find the strain energy stored in a wire with stress 2×10⁸ Pa, strain 0.002 and volume 5×10⁻⁵ m³.
Answer:  Density u = ½σ·ε = ½(2×10⁸)(0.002) = 2×10⁵ J/m³. U = u×V = 2×10⁵×5×10⁻⁵ = 10 J.
⚡ Shortcut:  U = ½σ·ε·V.
Example:  10 J stored.
Q11. Explain why a rubber band feels warm when stretched and cools on release.

Answer:  Stretching increases molecular order (and lowers entropy); releasing lets the molecules gain entropy and the temperature drop. Rubber's elasticity is largely entropy-driven, so mechanical work interconverts with heat.
⚡ Shortcut:  Rubber elasticity ≈ entropic (temperature rises on stretch).
Example:  Snap a band fast; it is warmer for a moment.
Q12. A 20 N load stretches a spring by 4 cm. Find the force constant and stored energy.
⚡ Shortcut:  k = F/x ; U = ½kx².
Example:  500 N/m, 0.4 J.
